name: Prochlorperazine (Compazine, Compro)
summary: A first-generation antipsychotic (phenothiazine) that’s mostly used for nausea—but it has older, rarely-used psychiatric indications (schizophrenia, anxiety). High side effect risk (EPS, sedation, low blood pressure), so it’s not a modern first-line psych med.
description: Prochlorperazine is a dopamine-blocking medication. In psychiatry, it’s an older antipsychotic that can reduce severe agitation or psychotic symptoms, and it has a labeled anxiety indication that’s largely outdated. The tradeoff is side effects: sleepiness, dizziness, restlessness/akathisia, muscle stiffness, tremor, and rare but dangerous reactions like neuroleptic malignant syndrome. In older adults—especially dementia—antipsychotics can raise the risk of stroke and death, so this med is generally avoided there.
patient_summary: Prochlorperazine is a dopamine-blocking medication. In psychiatry, it’s an older antipsychotic that can calm severe psychosis or agitation, and it has a labeled anxiety use that most clinicians don’t rely on anymore. The downside is side effects: sedation, dizziness, low blood pressure, and movement symptoms like restlessness or stiffness. It’s usually not a first-choice psychiatric medication today, especially in older adults or anyone at risk for falls or dementia-related complications.

primary_indications: Schizophrenia (legacy use; not a modern first-line option)
Anxiety (labeled, but largely replaced by safer modern treatments)

linked_conditions.context: Labeled indication, but it’s an older typical antipsychotic with a higher risk of movement side effects. Modern guidelines usually prefer newer antipsychotics unless there’s a specific reason.
Listed as a labeled use historically, but contemporary anxiety guidelines generally do not recommend prochlorperazine due to side effects and safer alternatives.
May be used in urgent settings to calm severe agitation, but it’s not a preferred first-line choice compared with more commonly used agents due to EPS and hypotension risk.

contraindications: Coma or severe CNS depression (eg, large amounts of alcohol, opioids, barbiturates)
Use in infants and children <2 years or <9 kg
Pediatric postoperative nausea/vomiting management (contraindicated in labeling)
Do not use for dementia-related psychosis (not approved; increased mortality risk in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotics)

efficacy_response.patient_text: For psychiatric use, prochlorperazine is considered a legacy medication. While dopamine-blocking effects can reduce psychosis or severe agitation, modern practice usually favors other antipsychotics because this one is more likely to cause movement side effects and sedation.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Oral absorption is limited; clinical effects may still occur quickly
pharmacokinetics.onset: Oral: ~30-40 minutes; IM: ~10-20 minutes; Rectal: ~60 minutes
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: Variable; peak antiemetic effect with IV reported ~30-60 minutes
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Primarily hepatic (active metabolite reported: N-desmethyl prochlorperazine)

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Prochlorperazine is mostly known as a nausea medication, but it’s technically a first-generation antipsychotic. In psychiatry, it’s a legacy option—meaning it exists on paper, but it’s not what most modern clinicians reach for first because side effects can be rough.
items: {link:condition:schizophrenia:Schizophrenia}: Can reduce hallucinations, delusions, and severe thought disturbance (older, less-preferred option today)
{link:condition:anxiety:Anxiety}: Labeled historically, but modern guidelines generally don’t recommend it due to better and safer choices
off_label: Acute agitation (urgent calming, usually not first choice)
Short-term sedation when severe symptoms require rapid quieting (risk/benefit has to be very carefully weighed)

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: This med tends to feel like a blunt instrument: it can quiet things down, but it can also make people feel heavy, foggy, or physically uncomfortable.

quotes: My brain got quieter fast—like the noise dropped a few notches.
It didn’t make me happy. It just made me less spun up.
It helped me stop escalating, but I felt kind of flat.
I felt sleepy and a little wobbly.
It hit like a wave of drowsiness.
I could function, but everything felt slower.
items.note: Sedation and dizziness can show up early, especially after injections or dose increases.

quotes: My body felt like it couldn’t sit still—like internal jittery panic.
I wanted to crawl out of my skin.
Mentally calmer, physically restless. Weird combo.
items.note: Akathisia is a classic dopamine-blocker side effect and can feel like anxiety—so it can confuse the picture.

quotes: My jaw felt tight and my body felt stiff.
I felt shaky and rigid, like my movements weren’t smooth.
It helped symptoms, but the physical side effects were not subtle.
items.note: These movement side effects are more likely with higher doses, longer use, and in older adults.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Prochlorperazine can kick in pretty quickly, especially by injection. The calming/sedating effects may appear early, but the tradeoff is that side effects can also show up fast.
key_points: Oral: ~30-40 minutes to start feeling effects
IM: ~10-20 minutes to start feeling effects
Rectal: ~60 minutes to start feeling effects
Half-life: ~6-10 hours after a single dose (longer with repeated dosing)

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: For psychiatric treatment, prochlorperazine is mostly a legacy option. Dopamine blockade can reduce psychosis and severe agitation in some people, but the side effect profile makes it a less common choice compared with newer antipsychotics.
sections.clinical_details: This medication’s psychiatric indications exist historically, but contemporary guidelines generally do not prioritize it for anxiety management or as a preferred antipsychotic for schizophrenia due to tolerability concerns (especially EPS, sedation, orthostatic hypotension, and anticholinergic effects).

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Avoid use for behavioral symptoms of dementia unless there’s a serious safety risk and non-med options failed. Antipsychotics in dementia are linked to increased mortality.
sections.black_box: Elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotic drugs are at an increased risk of death. Prochlorperazine is not approved for the treatment of patients with dementia-related psychosis.
other: Movement disorders (EPS): akathisia, dystonia, parkinsonism, and tardive dyskinesia (which can be irreversible)
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS): rare, life-threatening reaction with fever, rigidity, confusion, and autonomic instability
Sedation and CNS depression: higher fall and injury risk, especially in older adults and when combined with other sedatives
Orthostatic hypotension: dizziness, fainting, fall risk (especially with IV/IM dosing)
Cardiac conduction effects and arrhythmia risk: caution with QT risk and heart disease
Anticholinergic effects: confusion, constipation, urinary retention, blurry vision, dry mouth (especially in older adults)
Blood dyscrasias (rare but serious): leukopenia, neutropenia, agranulocytosis—monitor if risk factors exist
Aspiration risk: antipsychotics can be associated with swallowing issues and aspiration, especially in older adults
patient_counseling: If you feel intense inner restlessness, muscle spasms, a stiff jaw/neck, or unusual movements—tell your clinician ASAP. Don’t just ‘push through it.’
If you develop high fever, severe stiffness, confusion, or a racing pulse—this is an emergency (possible NMS).
Stand up slowly. This med can drop blood pressure and make you faint, especially early on or after injections.
Avoid alcohol and other sedatives unless your prescriber explicitly okays it—stacking sedatives increases fall and breathing risks.
In older adults (especially dementia), this medication can be dangerous. Use should be very deliberate and regularly reassessed.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: The big issues are sedation, dizziness/low blood pressure, and movement side effects (EPS). These can look like anxiety or agitation, which is frustrating because it can feel like the problem got worse when it’s actually a side effect.
plain_language_list: Restlessness (akathisia) that can feel like anxiety
Dry mouth, constipation, blurry vision, trouble urinating (anticholinergic effects)
Low blood pressure when standing (orthostatic hypotension)
Rare but serious: tardive dyskinesia, NMS, heart rhythm problems, severe blood count problems

common.patient_note: Can feel like heavy tiredness, slowed thinking, and poor coordination. This is a major fall risk in older adults and anyone combining other sedatives.

common.incidence: Frequency not defined (risk increases with IV administration, younger age, pregnancy, and higher dopamine blockade)
common.patient_note: Feels like you can’t sit still and your body is buzzing. It can be mistaken for worsening anxiety, but it’s a medication effect and needs a different fix.

common.incidence: Frequency not defined (higher risk in younger patients and males)
common.patient_note: Sudden painful stiffness—jaw/neck/eyes can be involved. This is treatable but urgent. If it happens, call your clinician or seek urgent care.

common.incidence: Frequency not defined (higher risk with older age and longer exposure)
common.patient_note: Tremor, stiffness, slowed movement. May fade after stopping, but it can linger for weeks or longer.
Lightheadedness when standing. Risk increases with parenteral dosing, older age, higher doses, and certain heart/blood pressure meds.
Dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurry vision, and confusion—especially in older adults.

serious: Tardive dyskinesia: involuntary movements (face/tongue/limbs) that may be irreversible, especially with higher cumulative dose and longer duration
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS): fever, severe rigidity, confusion, unstable blood pressure/heart rate (MEDICAL EMERGENCY)
Severe arrhythmias/conduction changes: palpitations, fainting, chest symptoms—seek urgent evaluation
Agranulocytosis or severe neutropenia: infection risk with fever/sore throat—requires immediate evaluation
Seizures (risk increases with seizure history or meds that lower seizure threshold)
Aspiration events (especially in older adults with swallowing risk)

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Prochlorperazine stacks side effects with other sedating, anticholinergic, or heart-rhythm–affecting medications. It can also interfere with dopamine-based Parkinson’s meds.

items.with: Alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines, sleep meds, sedating antihistamines
items.risk: Additive CNS depression: worse sedation, impaired breathing/alertness, falls, accidents.
items.action: Avoid combining when possible. If combination is unavoidable, use the lowest effective doses and monitor closely for excessive sedation and safety issues.

items.risk: Higher EPS and tardive dyskinesia risk; higher NMS risk.
items.action: Avoid duplicate dopamine blockade unless there’s a very clear reason and careful monitoring.

items.risk: Can counteract Parkinson’s treatment and worsen movement symptoms.
items.action: Avoid when possible; coordinate with neurology if Parkinson’s disease is in the picture.

items.with: QT-prolonging medications (multiple antidepressants, antipsychotics, antibiotics, antiarrhythmics)
items.risk: Increased risk of dangerous heart rhythm problems, especially with electrolyte abnormalities.
items.action: Review QT risk before combining. Consider ECG monitoring and correct potassium/magnesium if needed.

items.with: Anticholinergic medications (diphenhydramine, tricyclics, some bladder meds)
items.risk: More constipation, urinary retention, confusion, blurred vision—especially in older adults.
items.action: Use the minimum necessary and monitor bowel/bladder function and mental status.
Monitor orthostatics and counsel about slow position changes; consider dose adjustments.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: If prochlorperazine is being used for psychiatric symptoms (rare in modern practice), don’t stop abruptly after sustained use without a plan. A gradual taper helps reduce rebound symptoms and lowers the chance of withdrawal-like agitation or symptom relapse.
key_points: Short-term or intermittent use: Many people can stop without a formal taper, but side effects (sedation, dizziness) can still linger briefly.
Longer-term antipsychotic use: Taper gradually—often by small dose reductions every 1-2 weeks (or slower if symptoms return).
If akathisia is present: Stopping suddenly can feel awful; tapering and targeted treatment can make discontinuation more tolerable.
If tardive dyskinesia emerges: Don’t just ‘wait it out.’ Prompt reassessment is needed; earlier changes improve the odds of improvement.
If used in older adults: Deprescribing attempts are typically recommended to confirm ongoing need and minimize harm, unless symptoms are dangerous.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Psychiatric dosing exists, but this is not a commonly recommended psychiatric medication today. If it’s used for mental health symptoms, it should be at the lowest effective dose with careful monitoring for movement side effects, sedation, low blood pressure, and confusion—especially in older adults.

adult.anxiety_max: 20 mg/day; do not use longer than 12 weeks for anxiety
adult.schizophrenia_oral_initial: 5 to 10 mg PO 3 to 4 times daily
adult.schizophrenia_oral_titration: May increase every 2 to 3 days based on response and tolerability
adult.schizophrenia_oral_typical: 50 to 75 mg/day PO in divided doses (some patients may require higher)
adult.schizophrenia_oral_max: Up to 150 mg/day PO (specialist-level risk/benefit monitoring)
adult.schizophrenia_im_initial: 10 to 20 mg IM once; may repeat based on response and tolerability every 1 to 4 hours
adult.schizophrenia_im_maintenance_if_needed: If continued IM dosing is needed: 10 to 20 mg IM every 4 to 6 hours; transition to oral as soon as possible

sections.simple_explanation: For anxiety, prochlorperazine is an older approach and generally not recommended today because side effects can outweigh benefits. For schizophrenia, dosing is divided through the day, and injections may be used short-term in urgent situations—then switched to oral dosing as soon as possible.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: This medication is higher-risk in older adults and dementia. In pregnancy, antipsychotics are a shared decision-making situation—balancing relapse risk vs medication risk. For breastfeeding, data for prochlorperazine specifically are limited, but related phenothiazines can enter milk.
sections.pregnancy: Antipsychotic exposure data for first-generation antipsychotics as a class do not show a clear major malformation signal overall, but individual-drug data and long-term neurodevelopment data are limited. Third-trimester exposure to antipsychotics can lead to newborn EPS and/or withdrawal-like symptoms (agitation, feeding issues, tone changes, respiratory distress, sleepiness, tremor). Do not taper late in pregnancy solely to prevent newborn symptoms; instead, use the lowest effective dose and avoid polypharmacy when possible.
sections.lactation: It is not known if prochlorperazine is present in human milk. Other phenothiazines can be excreted in breast milk, so monitor the infant for sedation, poor feeding, or unusual sleepiness if exposure occurs. Use the lowest effective dose and consider alternatives when feasible.
sections.pediatrics: Avoid in children <2 years or <9 kg. In pediatric patients, use the lowest possible dose due to higher risk of extrapyramidal reactions and sedation. Movement reactions can be dramatic (eg, oculogyric crisis, torticollis).
sections.geriatrics: High-risk medication in older adults. Avoid for behavioral problems of dementia or delirium unless nonpharmacologic options failed and there is risk of harm. Antipsychotics in dementia are associated with increased stroke, cognitive decline, and mortality. If used, start at the low end of the adult range, titrate slowly, reassess frequently, and attempt deprescribing when clinically appropriate.
sections.hepatic: No specific manufacturer dose adjustment is provided, but systemic exposure may be increased because the drug is hepatically metabolized. Use caution, start low, and monitor for sedation, hypotension, and EPS.
sections.renal: No dosage adjustment is generally necessary (minimal renal clearance). Use caution in medically fragile patients due to hypotension and CNS effects rather than renal clearance.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Mental status and alertness: sedation, confusion, worsening cognition—especially in older adults
Movement side effects (EPS): check at every visit; reassess after initiation and dose changes; consider formal scales when risk is high
Tardive dyskinesia: screen regularly (at least annually; more often if high risk or symptoms appear)
Blood pressure and orthostatics: especially with parenteral dosing, older age, or fainting/fall risk
Fall risk: reassess regularly in adults ≥60 and anyone with dizziness, sedation, or prior falls
Cardiac risk: review QT risk factors and consider ECG monitoring when clinically indicated (especially with other QT-prolonging meds)
CBC: as clinically indicated, especially with preexisting low WBC or history of drug-induced leukopenia/neutropenia
Electrolytes, renal and liver function: as clinically indicated (particularly if medically complex or on multiple meds)
Prolactin-related symptoms: ask about menstrual changes, libido changes, galactorrhea, gynecomastia, erectile/ejaculatory issues; check prolactin if symptomatic
Metabolic monitoring: weight/BMI trend (even though this is not the most metabolic-heavy antipsychotic, baseline and periodic checks still matter in real life)

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Psychiatric use typically involves oral tablets or IM injections in urgent situations. Rectal and some injectable products exist mainly for nausea/vomiting use, but the dosage forms are still part of what’s available in practice.
items: Injection solution (as edisylate; strength expressed as base): 10 mg/2 mL (common)

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Prochlorperazine blocks dopamine receptors (especially D2) in the brain. Dopamine blockade can reduce psychotic symptoms and also produces anti-nausea effects by acting on the brain’s chemoreceptor trigger zone. It also has alpha-adrenergic and anticholinergic effects, which is why it can cause low blood pressure, dizziness, dry mouth, constipation, and confusion.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: In modern psychiatry, prochlorperazine is rarely a first-choice medication. For schizophrenia and related psychotic disorders, clinicians usually choose other antipsychotics that are better studied and often better tolerated. For anxiety, this medication is considered outdated because the side effect burden is high compared with modern options. If it shows up in psychiatric care today, it’s usually in unusual situations—short-term symptom control, special circumstances, or when other options aren’t feasible—and it requires careful monitoring.

seo.title: Prochlorperazine (Compazine): Psychiatric Uses, Dosing, Side Effects & Warnings
seo.description: Prochlorperazine (Compazine/Compro) is a first-generation antipsychotic mostly used for nausea, with legacy psychiatric uses (schizophrenia, anxiety). Learn dosing, sedation and EPS risks, dementia boxed warning, interactions, and monitoring.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.a: Yes. It’s a first-generation (typical) antipsychotic in the phenothiazine family. Most people know it as a nausea medication, but pharmacologically it’s a dopamine-blocker, which is the core mechanism of many antipsychotics.

It has a historical labeled anxiety indication, but in modern practice it’s usually not recommended for anxiety because the side effect burden (sedation, dizziness, movement symptoms) is higher than safer, more effective options.
Oral dosing can start working in about 30 to 40 minutes. IM injections can start working in about 10 to 20 minutes. Rectal dosing may take around an hour. Side effects can show up just as quickly.

faqs.q: What’s the biggest psychiatric side effect to watch for?
faqs.a: Movement side effects (EPS), especially akathisia. Akathisia can feel like internal panic or unbearable restlessness and is often mistaken for worsening anxiety—so it’s important to recognize it as a medication effect.

Yes. Like other dopamine-blocking antipsychotics, it can cause tardive dyskinesia—abnormal involuntary movements that may be irreversible. Risk rises with higher cumulative dose, longer duration, older age, and other risk factors.

faqs.q: What is the dementia warning about?
faqs.a: Antipsychotics used in older adults with dementia-related psychosis are associated with an increased risk of death compared with placebo in clinical trials. Prochlorperazine is not approved for dementia-related psychosis, and use for behavioral symptoms of dementia is generally avoided unless there’s a serious safety risk and non-med approaches failed.

faqs.q: Can prochlorperazine make you sleepy or dizzy?
faqs.a: Absolutely. Sedation and dizziness are common, and it can also cause orthostatic hypotension (blood pressure drops when standing). That combination increases fall risk—especially in older adults.

faqs.q: Do I need to taper off prochlorperazine?
faqs.a: If it was used briefly, many people can stop without a formal taper. But if it’s been used regularly for psychiatric symptoms over time, tapering gradually is usually safer and more comfortable—especially if stopping triggers rebound agitation or symptom return.

faqs.q: What medications should not be mixed with it?
faqs.a: Be cautious with other sedatives (alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines, sleep meds), other dopamine blockers (higher EPS risk), and QT-prolonging medications (heart rhythm risk). Also, it can interfere with dopamine-based Parkinson’s medications.

faqs.q: Is it safe in pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: This is a shared decision-making situation. Class-level data for first-generation antipsychotics don’t show a clear major malformation signal overall, but newborn EPS/withdrawal-like symptoms can occur with third-trimester exposure. For breastfeeding, it’s not well established whether prochlorperazine is in human milk, but related phenothiazines can be, so infant sedation and feeding should be monitored if exposure happens.
